rationale: A wins because it keeps the third angle grounded in a real protagonist: “What a state fire agency wants from a satellite that spots ignitions in minutes” turns the MOU into a testable workflow story instead of pretending Helio already has a category. B’s “Can satellites cut wildfire detection from hours to minutes?” drifts into an invented baseline and a category story the update does not prove. A also refuses the wildfire-season peg and the “faster” claim cleanly; B catches many of the same holes, but decorates one of them.
gaps_in_A: “SpaceX and Planet Labs alumni raise $7M to put wildfire detection in orbit” is the safest first pitch, but it still leans hard on founder pedigree; without confirmed roles, it can collapse into alumni-label trivia.
“The agency's problem is not time-pressured” is honest, but it means the customer-story angle needs the unnamed agency badly. If the agency will not talk, this angle dies.

“target launch window, even a rough one” asks for the right proof, but A could be firmer that no disclosed launch date makes the funding-mechanics angle a seed-round process story, not a deployment story.
gaps_in_B: “Can satellites cut wildfire detection from hours to minutes?” invents “hours” as the current baseline. The update only says Helio claims it can alert faster than current systems.

“A new constellation says yes — eventually” overstates the company’s position. No satellite is in orbit, no launch date is disclosed, and “constellation” is not supported beyond planned small satellites.
“category-creation” is padded. One $7M seed, one unnamed MOU, and no operating results do not make a category story without outside evidence.
“existing weather/imaging satellites” may be plausible context, but it is not in the update. For this assignment, plausible is still an invented prop.
